title: Every Flight Is Grounded on Day Trump Admin Installed AI Controls
content:
Every Flight Is Grounded on Day Trump Admin Installed AI Controls
A message sent to air traffic control towers reads, “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a nationwide ground stop at all airports due to “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”
“All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice,” an air traffic control advisory posted Friday afternoon read. “Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis.”
The nationwide ground stop took effect at 3:54 p.m. EST Friday and is scheduled to remain in effect until 11 p.m. The order allows flights in the air to land, but flights on the ground cannot take off.
When the ground stop was announced, more than 1,000 flights were airborne and destined for U.S. airports, according to FlightRadar24.
Over 30,000 flight departures and arrivals were scheduled for the rest of the day, according to flight-tracking app Flighty. Over 1.5 million people were scheduled to be on flights departing after the ground stop, aviation data firm Cirium said.
Reuters reports that shortly before the FAA issued its ground stop order, it halted traffic in Chicago due to air traffic control communications issues.

Law enforcement officials have since told CNN there is no evidence of a cyberattack. Expert guests on the network theorized that a mishap with a new FAA system upgrade—“SMART,” a cloud-based, AI-supported air traffic management platform that was scheduled to go live on Friday—could be to blame.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took questions from reporters outside the White House on Friday afternoon, but had little additional information to offer.
“There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us,” he said. “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.”
Mullin insisted that all planes in the air are not in danger and that the ground stop is not the result of a terror attack. However, Mullin refused to rule out a cyberattack, and even incorrectly stated that this was the first ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks.
“We don’t want to get ahead of ourselves,” Mullin said. “Anytime something like this happens, I mean, the last time I believe that we’ve had a national ground stoppage was 9/11. Of course, in DHS, we’re getting a ton of calls saying, ‘Is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack?’ Everybody’s safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying or anything like that.”
Mullin struggled through the second half of his answer, saying, “As we investigate, um, what caused this, you always got to assume that as many cyberattacks that take place, that you make that assumption. So, but, as of right now, that’s not known. So we are, we’re going to continue to work—the first thing we want to do is make sure we restore the communications. We get all the flights on the ground, and then we, we get back normal operations. But we’re going to continue to work to find out what the root of the cause is.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X that the ground stop is due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Top congressional reporter Jake Sherman, of Punchbowl News, wrote on X that even “key lawmakers are in the dark at the moment about the ground stop.”
It is just the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001. The other occurred in January 2023, when the FAA paused domestic departures for about 90 minutes over a system outage.
In that case, conservatives like Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert and Donald Trump Jr. eagerly blamed then-Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg for the mess.
“This is what happens when you hire clueless liberals for jobs they aren’t qualified to do,” Boebert, who was ousted from Congress on Friday, wrote on X.
Trump Jr. added: “Yet another major blow to incompetent Transportation Sect Mayor Pete and people who get important jobs with no experience to check some identity politics boxes.”
Neither had publicly weighed in on Friday’s ground stop as of publication.
Friday’s ground stop should not impact the president’s travel plans. The White House announced Thursday that he would remain in Washington over the weekend and not make his typical weekend trip to Mar-a-Lago.
As of 10:30 p.m., more than six hours after the ground stop took effect, Trump hadn’t posted about it on Truth Social.
The ground stop comes less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year.
Duffy, during a press conference Friday night alongside Mullin, asked Congress for $50 billion to fix the issue.
“This is the greatest country—by the way, with the greatest president. Let’s give the money to fix this very real problem,” he said.
That didn’t go over well with former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene. She called his ask a “shakedown.”

report.summary: The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on the day a new AI-powered air traffic system was set to launch, sparking speculation about the cause.
report.background: The Federal Aviation Administration has been under pressure to modernize its aging air traffic control infrastructure. The Trump administration has pushed for increased privatization and technological upgrades, including AI integration. The new 'SMART' system—a cloud-based, AI-supported air traffic management platform—was scheduled to go live on Friday. This follows a January 2023 system outage that caused a 90-minute ground stop, and political blame games ensued. The FAA's systems have long been criticized as outdated, and the push for AI aims to improve efficiency and safety. However, integrating AI into critical infrastructure raises concerns about reliability, testing, and cybersecurity. The ground stop occurred less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel periods, heightening public scrutiny.
key_points: A nationwide ground stop was issued at 3:54 p.m. EST Friday, affecting over 30,000 scheduled flights and 1.5 million passengers. Inbound international flights were managed case-by-case, and flights in the air were allowed to land.

The ground stop coincided with the scheduled launch of the FAA's 'SMART' AI-supported air traffic management platform. Experts theorized that a mishap with the new system could be to blame, though no official confirmation was given.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated there was no evidence of a cyberattack, calling it a 'telecommunication outage,' but refused to rule out a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited a 'communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.'

It was only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11, the first being a January 2023 system outage. Political reactions included a $50 billion funding request from Duffy and criticism from Marjorie Taylor Greene, who called it a 'shakedown.'
report.impact: The incident underscores the high stakes of integrating AI into critical infrastructure. For the AI industry, it highlights the need for rigorous testing, fail-safes, and transparency before deployment. Developers are reminded of the importance of robust error handling and redundancy, especially in systems where failures can cause widespread disruption. For regular users, the ground stop caused significant travel chaos and raised concerns about the reliability of AI-driven systems. It may accelerate calls for stricter regulation and oversight of AI in safety-critical domains, and could erode public trust if the connection to the AI system is confirmed.
report.tools: For real-time flight tracking, FlightRadar24 and Flighty were used during the ground stop. Those interested in AI safety can explore open-source frameworks like AI Safety Gridworlds or tools for formal verification of AI systems. ADS-B Exchange provides crowdsourced flight data for monitoring air traffic.
